issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile is not well aligned with the cognitive formulation. The only active edge is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from the selected appraisals. Overeating and busyness can follow from distressing appraisals, but 'Checking Surroundings' is a threat-monitoring/safety behavior that usually implies an active Threat component or a strong Trigger/Threat linkage, both of which are absent in the formulation and not represented elsewhere in the self-report.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm' is a global current-danger appraisal that typically pairs with a Threat presentation and supports behaviors like environmental scanning. But Threat is not represented as an active component in the formulation, and the rest of the negative appraisals are more about self-doubt and shattered assumptions. This makes the appraisal/strategy pattern clinically incoherent for the specified edge structure.

vignette: Mr. Thomas had always taken pride in his work as a delivery driver. For over four decades, he'd navigated the busy streets of New York City with precision and care, delivering packages to various businesses and homes. His routine was comforting, providing a sense of structure and purpose that anchored him through life's ups and downs. However, everything changed one fateful evening last summer when Thomas encountered an assailant during his delivery route. As he parked his van in a dimly lit alleyway to make a drop-off at a small warehouse, someone approached from behind and attacked him without warning. The attacker struck Thomas multiple times before fleeing into the night. Terrified and bruised, Thomas managed to call for help but was left shaken by the experience. In the weeks following the assault, Thomas struggled with intense feelings of anxiety and distress. He began overeating as a way to manage his emotions, finding solace in the comfort provided by food. The pounds piled on, straining his health and relationships. His wife, Margaret, grew concerned about his well-being but didn't understand why he was turning to food for relief. Thomas also threw himself into work, becoming busier than ever before. He worked extra hours and even took additional deliveries when possible, all in an effort to avoid the thoughts that haunted him. The more he worked, the less time he had to dwell on what happened. However, his increasing workload began to take a toll on both his physical health and their social life as a couple. Margaret noticed that Thomas seemed distant and preoccupied, often canceling plans to work late. Despite these coping mechanisms, memories of the assault continued to intrude upon his daily life. He tried desperately to suppress thoughts about the event but found it nearly impossible. The more he attempted to push away the traumatic memory, the more vividly it resurfaced. Simple triggers like dark alleys or unlit areas would send him into a panic, causing him to avoid certain routes during deliveries. Thomas had come to believe that he couldn't trust himself to do the right thing, especially in dangerous situations. His self-doubt made every decision feel uncertain and fraught with potential failure. This pervasive sense of doubt also extended to his beliefs about the world-what once seemed like a predictable place now felt unpredictable and unsafe. One evening, as Thomas was making deliveries near the warehouse where the assault occurred, he found himself trembling uncontrollably. The sight of the familiar alleyway brought back vivid images of that night, and he nearly had a panic attack on the spot. Realizing he could no longer handle these intense reactions alone, Thomas finally decided to seek help. What frightened him most was the possibility of reliving those terrifying moments again and again without any relief. He was certain that if he did not address his symptoms, they would continue to worsen, potentially affecting his job and his relationship with Margaret. Thomas hoped that through therapy, he could regain some sense of control over his life and find a way to trust himself and the world once more. Margaret supported him in this decision, recognizing how much her husband had been struggling. As Thomas stepped into the therapist's office for the first time, he felt a mix of fear and hope-afraid of confronting what happened but hopeful that with support, he could begin to heal from the trauma.
